utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I should like to say good morning to all those present in the courtroom, to the Prosecution, the Defence, the accused, and our registrar who is back with us this morning. We're going to carry on with our proceedings with another witness. The witness is present in the courtroom, so we're going to move into private session straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Madam Egels, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours, good morning, everybody. In 1993, the witness lived with her family in Visici, in the municipality of Capljina. Around the 15th of April, 1993, HVO soldiers came to her house to arrest her husband but did not find him. Around the 20th of April, soldiers searched her house for weapons. Since 15 April, 1993, the HVO kept arresting Muslim men that were taken to Dretelj or Gabela. On the 1st of July, 1993, the HVO arrested all Muslim men in Visici regardless of their civilian or military status, their health, or their age. At the end of July, 1993, the mosque in Visici was destroyed. On 11 August, 1993, the witness, together with other women and children, was arrested by the Capljina MUP and taken to Tasovcici where they were kept in a private house. Later in August other women were brought to that house in Tasovcici. The civilians confined there were interrogated by members of the MUP and SIS. On the 2nd of October, 1993, the witness was transferred by the police to Silos in Capljina where the conditions of detention were terrible. At the Silos, the witness saw two men being taken away and come back beaten. She heard them being beaten. She also witnessed women being taken out and was told they were made to walk around naked. Detainees were tormented mentally and physically. On the 11th or 12th of October, 1993, Muslim men detained in Gabela were brought to the Silos in order to hide them from the Red Cross who was visiting Gabela. On the 19th of October, the witness was transferred to the students' dormitory in Capljina because the Silos had become too sold for the children who were confined there. She stayed at the students' dormitory until the 10th of June, 1994, when she was released with the intervention of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness CN.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: On the 29th of March, 2001, you provided a statement to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecution of this Tribunal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: At the time you provided this statement, did you provide it truthfully?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Did you answer the questions freely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: At the conclusion of this interview were you read back your statement in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Did you then sign the English version of that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you to turn to Exhibit number 9754.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And for that purpose, Your Honour, can we go into private session and this document being under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness CN, when we met yesterday with myself and an investigator, were you given an opportunity to read your statement in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Is it correct that upon reviewing that statement in your language you wanted to make some -- well, two minor corrections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Is it correct that on page 2, paragraph 9 of the English statement, page 3, paragraph 3 of the Bosnian version, you specified that the mosque in Visici was destroyed in July, and the year was 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And on page 3, paragraph 8 of the English statement, page 5, paragraph 1 of the Bosnian version, when you stated -- you stated that the sentence, "I recognised the policemen that came to the house. One was (first name unknown) Konjcanin and another one from Celjevo whose name I don't know," should be replaced by, "I recognised the policemen who came to the house. One was from Konjic, another one from Celjevo. I don't know their names."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: If you had to provide today to this court a full testimony, would the content of that testimony be the same as the content of your written statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness CN, I would like you to turn now to Exhibit number 1900 in the bundle in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I might intervene, not to waste time later on for practical reasons. On page 6, line 21, it says that the witness confirmed that the mosque in Visici was destroyed in July and that the year was 1993, and last night, late last night, we received a correction where it says that it was in June. Now, I don't know whether it is the transcript that's the problem or -- I apologise, but I've been informed that another correction was received this morning to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That did not escape my notice, because I saw that there was June and July. So, madam, when was the mosque destroyed, in June, 1993, or in July, 1993, to the best your recollections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In July. The seventh month, July.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness CN, coming back to Exhibit number 1900. In your statement you referred to HVO soldiers that came to your house around the 15th of April, 1993, in order to arrest your husband who was a member of the ABiH. This document is an order by Commander Obradovic dated the 16th of April, 1993. I would like you to turn to item 2, page 1 of both the English and Bosnian version of this document. On that item it is written: "Order. All members of the BiH army carrying BiH army insignias are to be arrested immediately and detained for 15 days." What that paragraph states, does it correspond to what you experienced on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to turn to Exhibit number 3057. In your statement you refer to the arrest of Muslim men in your village on the 1st of July, 1993. Can I ask you to turn to page 2, paragraph 2 of the Bosnian version. And that is page 3, paragraph 1 of the English version under the header, "Security-related events." Does this correspond to what you perceived on the ground? This paragraph refers to taking Muslim men eligible for military service and it's an order of 1st of July, 1993. Does this correspond to what you perceived on the ground on the 1st of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: There were many more people than the 161 persons mentioned here, because they were collecting up all the military-able men at the time, and among them there were also children and elderly persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Witness, can I ask you now to turn to Exhibit number 9086. This is a series of photographs. Do you recognise these locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Silo in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: For the record the first page of that bundle. What about the second page of that bundle? Do you recognise that location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is also the Silo. It's where we went in, where we entered the Silo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: The third page of that bundle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I went in and out on -- by the other door, it seems to me that the entrance is right, the far end, but I don't -- I can't make out what side it is, but it is the Silo building.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: What about the fourth page of that bundle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never went through that door, as far as I remember. I know that there were some steps, and this seems familiar. Number 2, photograph number 2 is familiar. But it is the Silo, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: And the last page of that bundle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Can I ask you now to turn to Exhibit number 9285. Do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the mosque in Visici that existed before the war and that was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: What about the next page of that bundle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's also the mosque taken from a different angle.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness CN.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Egels. I have a question for you. You showed the witness photographs. There were some that she recognised and others that she did not. Now, during the proofing session did you show the witness the photographs or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So why show her photographs which she does not recognise? Wouldn't it have been better not to have shown her those photographs, the ones she did not recognise? And we would have saved time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EGELS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas seems to be approving. Now, with respect to the Silo, a number of witnesses have already said yes, that is the Silo, they recognised it. So there we have it. But any way thank you, madam. I have a short question for you, Witness, not a complicated one. You said a moment ago that you recognised the policemen. One was from Konjic and the other from Celjevo, but you said you said you didn't know their names. Now, how can you recognise policemen and know that they were from two different localities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Celjevo is right by Visici. It's the neighbouring village following on from one another, so I know all those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So they were policemen that you already knew.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before they came to arrest you, those individuals had already been policemen? They were already policemen, or did you realise they were policemen the day they came to arrest you and your perhaps knew them in a different capacity previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's like this, you see: When we were taken away, taken out of our houses to Dino Trajlovic -- Tasovic's [phoen] house there was a police car and there was a policeman who had been a policeman before as well. He was a policeman before and at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they came in a police car, and it was the police car that you knew, you recognised.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you. Now, another query. To the best of your recollection, these policemen, were they civilian policemen from the MUP or were they military police? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The civilian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I turn to the Defence teams. Who is going to start off, as usual I'm going to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President; good morning Your Honours; good morning madam. We have no questions for this witness and we wish to thank her for coming here to give her evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Next. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, according to our order for this morning, the -- General Praljak's Defence comes first, and General Praljak himself would like to ask the witness a few questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, madam. My name is Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to 1992, and then I have a question regarding the mosque. Is it true and correct that in 1992 Visici were bombed by the air by the Yugoslav People's Army air force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Is it also true and correct -- or, rather, do you know that at that time in 1992 the Serbs took control of the entire area of Stolac right up to the river Neretva in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Dubrava and Stolac areas, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as the bombing of all these localities, including your village, continued, you in your statement say that you left with your young child and went to Croatia where you spent two and a half months. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Grac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In Grac. Right. Now, did anybody force you to return or could you stay in Gradac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought I could return, yes. I went voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So you thought that after those people were liberated that you could live there normally later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went back on my own responsibility. I knew what was waiting there for me, but I decided to go back home nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And you say, "when the Bregava Brigade of the BH army was formed my husband joined up."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did anybody prevent him? Was it on a voluntary basis? Could he just have a normal choice? The brigade functioned normally and he had this choice, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was his choice, his own choice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. Yes. It was his choice. And that was 1992, the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was 1993. I'm sorry, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I need you to clarify something, given the question that's just been put to you. You said in response to General Praljak's question that after the Serbian shelling you had left your village to go to Croatia. Can you tell me, when were you actually staying in Croatia, from which month until which month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From April, 1992. I stayed there for two and a half months. I was there in April and May for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And when you were in Croatia, you could move around freely in Croatian territory? You weren't controlled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I was free to move around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And when you decided at the end of May or the beginning of June, since you said you stayed there for two months, when you decided to return to your village you were free to decide to return? You did that voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, voluntarily, although it was a risk at the time when I returned with my child. Many did not return. It was really a decision that I myself took.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that others didn't take the same decision. Do you know why or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, some people didn't feel safe. Some didn't want to. It was their affair. I know as far as I'm concerned I decided to return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said they didn't feel safe. Because of the Serbs, or because of others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know what it's like in war. You never know what will happen. One moment you're in free territory, the next moment you're not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could we say that it's more likely that you returned in June, 1993, because that's when the Dubrava plateau was liberated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in 1992. But my husband didn't join the army in 1992, as you said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No. I didn't say that. Madam, that's not what I said. I don't know about that. But let's finish this part about Croatia. Those others who were still afraid, you didn't know whether the territory was safe. They could freely remain in Croatia. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Do you know that the Bregava Brigade was formed of Muslims? That's what we called them at the time. Towards the end of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Your husband voluntarily joined the Bregava Brigade which was at Gubavica. That was his choice, and no one prevented him from doing that? ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how he -- that's what he decided.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In your statement, page 4 of your statement, you say, "Sometime in July, 1993, two Croats arrived at my house, and they were smuggling people to Croatia."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did this for money. They would cross the border.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: So we had these smugglers who were earning money because of the fate people were meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's their affair.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: When you would cross over into Croatia -- those who crossed over to Croatia they still had the status of refugees. They were free to move around Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Later on it was more difficult.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It was more difficult to cross over into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not only to cross over into Croatia, but to be in Croatia. It was always possible for you to be arrested. This was all the personal decision of one individual, but the risk was real. There was a risk.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I don't understand. In Croatia -- well, there were over 500 or 600.000 refugees in Croatia. People had been registered. They'd been provided with accommodation. So I don't know who was arresting people. Are you aware of any examples of someone arresting others, women, children, men? Unless we're talking about crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was different in 1992. In 1993, everything changed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In 1993, in June, everything changed. Everything changed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but what changed in Croatia? Tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the experience of others, I know that they travelled to Zagreb in a state of fear, and they didn't feel safe in Zagreb. As to who arrested them or who performed such arrests, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I apologise, but I have to clarify this issue. There were 3 or 400.000 refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina there at the time. So how was it possible for someone to arrest them and why didn't they feel safe in Zagreb? Who told you about? That whose experience is that? What can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look, I wasn't in Zagreb at the time. I personally can't say that I saw such things. Whatever I'm saying is based on hearsay. It's the experience that others had.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to ask you something else now. Can you tell me the exact date on which the mosque in your village was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I think it was towards the end of July. Perhaps the 17th, but I couldn't tell you the exact date. This happened on two occasions. The mosque was destroyed on one evening. Then there was a pause the next day, and then on the third evening the minaret was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And you think that was towards the end of July.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was not in June, it was in July.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: There's 30 days in July. Can you be a little bit more precise as to the date is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as of the 17th of June. I said towards the end of July. Believe me, when I gave this statement I couldn't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, you have no questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. I'd like to go back to a Prosecution document, P 01900. It's an order from the 1st HVO Knez Domagoj Brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It's an order dated the 16th of April, 1993, and it says that the entry of BH army members is not allowed into the area of responsibility of the brigade from the Rotimlje to Drenovac area. And item 2 says whoever fails to abide by the order will be arrested and detained for a 15-day period. Witness, in that area was the Knez Domagoj Brigade active and was the Bregava Brigade active? It was an ABiH unit. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably, but I couldn't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since you know that your husband was in the HVO and you also know since you yourself have said this, you also know that he fled to the ABiH, to the Bregava Brigade. Do you know that apart from those two units there was some other unit of some other army active in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people from Visici weren't in the Knez Domagoj Brigade. These people from Visici were in a special company. I don't know its exact name. The people from Visici had nothing to do with the Knez Domagoj Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was that unit an HVO unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's something I do know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we therefore conclude that in the area there was an HVO unit or, rather, HVO units that were active, and there was an ABiH brigade called the Bregava Brigade that was also active? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could this order therefore concern only members of the Bregava Brigade, the ABiH Bregava Brigade? Only they could have gone to that territory, and this order could concern them alone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't answer that question exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you have told me that there were no other ABiH units in the area --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look, I wasn't a member of the ABiH. I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, you said that the situation in the field was such as it has been described in this order, and that's why I'm analysing this order with you right now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look, all I know is that my husband was in the armija, and I'm not familiar with all these other matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, have a look at the bottom of the order. In the left-hand corner. Who was this order forwarded to? Read out item 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says the Bregava Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The Bregava Brigade. So it was forwarded to the ABiH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Since your husband was in both units, do you know that the HVO and the Bregava Brigade divide the zone of responsibility among themselves so the Bregava Brigade had full control of one area, whereas the HVO had control of another area. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. You can't put that question to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was an agreement reached by the HVO and the ABiH according to which members of the Bregava Brigade would not go to the territory under HVO control without having previously informed the HVO of the fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I had nothing to do with that. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know that individual members and groups of members of the Bregava Brigade went to the territory under the control of the HVO without having previously informed them of their arrival, as had been agreed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I know nothing about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: According to the information you have, was the possibility of detaining people for 15 days also valid for soldiers you believed were members of your own units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now let's have a look at another Prosecution document discussed by the witness, P 03057. You've found it, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you about the part my colleague from the Prosecution asked you about. You confirmed that what happened in the field corresponded to the description in the document under the part entitled "Matters of security interest." I'll ask you about this. We're talking about an order from the Knez Domagoj Brigade about bringing in individuals. It's dated the 1st of July, 1993, and it says that the order concerns the deterioration of the security situation in Mostar. You confirmed the contents of this part of the document, and, as a result, which events in Mostar are concerned in this document that talks about bringing in Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was in Bijelo Polje, as far as I can remember. These events took place in Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What happened in Bijelo Polje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. There was a conflict between the armija and HVO members as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what was the outcome of this clash?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was the outcome? Who won?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the armija, as far as I can remember. They just took that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. And as a result, the security situation in the area deteriorated; is that correct? That's what it says here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But they came to arrest on the 14th -- on the 15th of April, not on the 1st of July. That's when the arrests started, as far as I can remember. It wasn't on the 1st of July. On the 1st of July there were arrests on a large scale.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, we'll move on to April, 1993, later on. We're just discussing this order now. Since you have confirmed the truth of the contents of this order, I'm asking you about what you know about the information you have, that when the ABiH took Bijelo Polje the security situation deteriorated. What do you know about the deterioration of the security situation in that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on the 1st of July, in the morning, all the men were gathered. Not only those fit for military service. There were younger men 17 years of age, and there were elderly men too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, but these arrests were the result of the deterioration of the security situation described in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. We had nothing to do with that, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say "we," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I mean the people from Visici who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'd now like to ask you something about what you said in your written statement. With regard to your husband, you said that he was in the HVO until mid-March, 1993. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, look. I don't know the month. All I know is that he was in the Patriotic League and then in the HVO, and then he moved into the armija. Believe me, I don't know the exact date. I don't know the month.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your written statement you use the verb "fled" or "escaped" from the HVO. Why did you say that he escaped from the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, maybe that was a mistake. He transferred from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: He decided to join the armija. In your statement you also say that they kept calling him from the HVO and sent him letters but that he disregarded them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's about his affair. I suppose he knew why he disregarded them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the contents of those letters were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, since you say that he disregarded them, does that mean that they called him to return to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he probably had his own reasons for not going back to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, but did they invite him to come back? Did they call him to come back, regardless of his reasons not to respond to disregard them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I have to answer that? Well, I don't know. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Witness, do you know how the HVO behaved when some of its members failed to turn up to the unit and when he was absent for a certain amount of time? What was the standard procedure? What would be done in somebody's absence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You describe the situation and say that two uniformed HVO officers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't say officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: That's what it says in the written statement. But you meant soldiers, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I've been warned quite rightly that I was reading a portion of the statement and it slipped my mind that it might be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, make the order to strike that from the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we move into private session, then, because I'd like to discuss this portion of the witnesses statement.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As we were saying, these two soldiers turned up. They asked you whether your husband was at home. Your answer was that he was not, and they left. Is that right? Can you remember now whether it was standard practice that if a soldier didn't turn up to his unit that somebody from that unit would come by to see why the person was and sent, whether he was sick or anything else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not hear the -- he was not in any military unit at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I think we'll have to repeat the question and answer because there's been a slight misunderstanding. My question was, and the answer was not recorded, was this: Two HVO soldiers arrived at your house, asked about your husband's whereabouts. You said your husband wasn't at home, and they left. Is that right? A little louder, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but they were looking for his brother as well, who was not in any military unit at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My next question was this: Did you know -- do you know that if somebody was and sent from a unit that someone from the unit would come home to ask why the person was absent, whether they were sick or some other reason? But anyway, that is somebody would come by to see why a particular soldier hadn't turned up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Then we'll move on. Tell me, please, what was the HVO soldiers' conduct when they came by to ask about your husband and when they came looking for weapons and when later on they also came to your house? Did they believe you when you said, "No, my husband is not at home"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second time they came there were over 10 armed soldiers who enter the house without asking, without any warning, and they search the house, the yard, the garage, and they just went in without asking permission at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, would you approach the microphone so we can hear you better when you give us your answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When your husband was in the HVO, was he issued with any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, well, I don't remember him bringing any weapons home. I can't give you a precise answer to that question. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, do you know whether he returned his weapon to the HVO when he decided, as you say, to escape to the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did the HVO soldiers who came to search your house clearly state that they had come to look for weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they came to look for weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that there is a lot of noise in the courtroom and they find it difficult to hear the speakers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement you speak of numerous arrests that took place in mid-April, 1993; is that right? Can you tell us who was arrested? And if you know who was arrested, could you tell us whether they were a member of any army, whether they occupied any prominent position in your community, a be so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Am I allowed to mention names?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, if you want to name names, if you can name names, then --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps -- well, I don't know if we need to go into private session for people who were detained, but we can do so out of an abundance of caution perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Out of an abundance of caution, let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, these arrests at the beginning of July, 1993, I have some questions to ask you about them, and I'm interested in when you say that people who were over the age of 70 were arrested. Now, since the HVO order referred exclusively to military-able men, I would like to ask you for examples of what you said or -- can you ask you this way: Do you know the names of any persons who were over the age of 70 and who were arrested at that time? And then after your answer we can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say over 70. I said up to 70, up to age 70.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, do you know the name of anybody who was over the age of 60 when they were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Then may we go back into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you for -- for the time, Mr. President. First, before I address that, if I might make one slight observation with respect to the last question -- set of questions posed by Judge Prandler, because it's -- I've noticed that on a couple of previous occasions there have been some questions about people returning to their properties. That issue is an extremely complicated issue in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I have personally worked on the issue because I know how complicated it is. Out of -- if the question is being posed out of interest, I have no objections, but that is not a matter of the indictment, whether somebody has been able to return to their home at this particular point, because the issues could be a variety of issues. During a war or after the war people settled in and then, even if you want to move back to your place, somebody might be in there because he has no place to go and so on and so forth. Some folks decided not to return. So I just mention that as an observation. It's not a criticism. I'm just mentioning it because I do get alarmed that somehow that may creep into, you know, your factoring certain, you know, decisions at the end. With respect to my request yesterday, it seems that we are becoming more and more continental --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Karnavas, to clarify something you have just said. It's a very complex issue, that's true, but let's not forget that in the indictment, the indictment alleges that property, or, rather, flats that belonged to Muslims were flats from which their owners had been expelled so that Croats move in. So if a Judge reads such allegations in an indictment, the Judges will want to see whether these flats were perhaps requisitions or legally taken over, were they subsequently returned to their legitimate orders. That's what the Judges would like to find out. Were they returned as part of legal proceedings, as a result of legal proceedings? That's why the question was asked about whether legal proceedings had been instituted, or perhaps the government took certain measures to return such property to their owners. And this is an important issue and one that we have to address. And Judge Prandler also has something he would like to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I would like to thank Mr. Karnavas for responding to my question which I asked from the witness, and I took note of the -- of his explanation, and I'm sure he's a very good expert on it, that many, in a way, houses and properties had been -- changed hard, et cetera, during the last couple of years during the conflict, and that is why I only simply asked the question. And even if you recall, I did mention if they then moved to a house which was vacated previously by a Croat or other Serb family. So it was actually from this point of view which I asked for, in a way, a humanitarian point of view. But anyway, I thank you for raising this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And thank you very much, Judge Prandler for the additional explanation. Rest assured that there is a law on the return of abandoned property, that the Office of the High Representative has put into place, that it is harmonised throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. With respect to the procedures, it's quite evident that you know in this hybrid system that we're struggling to find new ways to be more efficient, and those of us who come from the Anglo-Saxon system, from the adversarial system, at points of time have had to make some adjustments, and we'll continue to make adjustments. But those of us who appreciate what is happening in court feel that there are ways that we could expedite the procedures given that, one, we don't have the strict rules of evidence we normally have with the admission of evidence because we don't have a jury. We have professional Judges. So from that standpoint we don't have to worry about tainting someone's mind. There is have very low threshold that we have to meet in order to introduce documents in. I think documents coming, especially from the HVO or the HZ HB or HR HB, I think by and large the Prosecution will be able to get all those documents in, assuming they don't have any particular obstacles with respect to where it was found or the authenticity of it. I say this because with the witnesses -- these 92 ter witnesses, it seems to me that the quickest way to resolve these issues is to simply have the witness give a very brief narration, if you will, of what happened, or the summary that is being read. If we have, say, 10 documents that we want to tender through this particular witness, if the Prosecution were to alert both us and the Trial Chamber the exact passages that they wish, in other words, because they're trying to marry, if you will, the testimony with the documents. Now, it doesn't make any sense to say does this -- is this consistent with, because you're professional Judges. You can read it. They will be able to make references to that in their final brief. But of course it would be helpful for them to point out to everybody exactly what passages they're relying on in order to connect and link up. That would allow the Defence then to target and focus their cross-examination on perhaps other areas of those documents that are not being mentioned, or perhaps to bring in other documents, or to ask specific questions. In other words -- and this is worked out in advance. And the Prosecution -- it's very clear that they're very well order and prepared. They know which documents they wish to bring in and which portions of the documents they wish to bring in with respect to the witness. I think if that was brought to our attention it early on, then we could probably do maybe three witnesses a day on these crime-base type of witnesses or these 92-base witnesses. So I think that's one way that we can speed up the process. And I don't think that either party would be disadvantaged because the primary basis for having a 92 bis or ter witness is to get their statement in. Then we can read it and so on and so forth. One other thing is, with respect to the proofing notes, which in my opinion because of this mixed system and it's an adversarial system and the Prosecution is not like an investigative judge and those statements do not carry the same weight as if they were from an investigative judge, it is only natural that the Prosecution would want to meet with the witness, refresh their memory and since there is the language problem to have the witness read the statement in their language and correct certain facts, and I think both parties benefit from that process. And I don't think it is being abused. Where there are corrections, it might be more efficient because yesterday I timed it, it was approximately 20 minutes to go through the corrections. No fault of the Prosecution or the witness. It's just a time-consuming aspect. We obviously get the version in English. It might be overly inconvenient to ask that the Prosecution translate that into B/C/S for the witness to also read and verify and sign, but I think if the Prosecution were to have one of their language assistants read back to the witness prior to the witness coming in the proofing sheet, then it -- one simple question could be, "Did you make some corrections?" "Yes." "And we read to you earlier on that corrections were on this paragraph, that paragraph, and so on," without necessarily going through the whole text. In other words, with one or two questions the witness would say, "yes," and then the proofing notes become also part of the witness's statement. Again, we could save probably -- at least with some witness, some time. Lastly, I've noticed that we're using a lot of photographs. The photographs have already come in. The places are identified so there is no real dilemma, on than perhaps where the Prosecution wishes to make sure that the witness can identify these particular barracks, lest there be any argument from the Defence that their witness is confabulating or wasn't there or so on and so forth. So I don't know have a problem with that. But I think showing -- yesterday there was a picture shown to a witness. It was a village. And the question was, "Can you point out where your house is?" And then we spent about -- and I timed it, about three or four minutes where the gentleman had to look and then mark, and so on and so forth. What benefit does this have in the long-run? Is his house at issue? No. So why bother to ask the witness to look at this photograph, try to identify his house, which was not even in the photograph, identifiably so, to mark us, just to have one more piece of evidence to bother -- for you to be bothered with. One photograph. What does this photograph reflect? It's the village. Boom. Why? Because it isn't at issue whether that person was from that particular village. Now, there are instances where the photographs are important and I think we can spend more valuable time on those instances. So constantly as we're going through this process at least I'm trying to find ways, given the system that we have, to ensure the rights of the accused, to make sure the Prosecution can get their case in. And if we can sort of find ways to bridge that gap and save some time, I think that may be a more efficient way. And as I said, we're going more continental and I don't have a problem with that but I think there are ways and there are benefits to be gained from that process, and I thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll summarise what you have just said. The three main issues, problems, that have been mentioned by Mr. Karnavas. Corrections to the written statements, first of all. Quite rightly, Mr. Karnavas pointed out that we waste a lot of time when reading out the corrections made by the witness. Mr. Karnavas suggests that there should be a note that would be attached to the statement, a proofing note. And as the witness is proofed before the hearing, this would be possible. The Defence, in order to avoid error, suggests that when the Prosecution meets the witness, you should be assisted by a language assistant and, given all the staff you have at your disposal, that should not pose much of a problem. And in this way you could save much time. Secondly, there are the documents shown to the witness. The questions concern the content of the documents, the paragraphs, et cetera. It would be good to identify the relevant paragraphs, to inform the Defence of the paragraphs identified and thus we would save time because the Defence would know in advance which paragraphs you would be questioning the witness about. And then thirdly, we have the problem of photographs. Numerous photographs are shown. For example, the photographs of the Silo. Perhaps About 30 such photographs have already been shown to various witnesses. It's not really necessary to continue showing such photographs. And then there it's question of whether the photograph is useful. To know whether the witness's house is in such-and-such a position, well, if it's not useful then it's really not necessary to do this. If it's useful because the witness could have seen the mosque or something from that position, well, then I guess it's useful. So these are three very interesting comments. I don't know whether Mr. Scott has had time to think about this. Are there any comments you'd like to make, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour the -- in terms of the documents I wanted to very measured in terms of my response because I appreciate constructive comments both from counsel and the Chamber. On the issue of documents, this is indeed a position that the Prosecution has been taking since before trial, that the admission of documentary evidence could be handled much more efficiently. In fact, it's the Prosecution's position that most of these documents shouldn't have to be put to a witness at all. And the reason we go through this exercise of showing them and asking them, "Is this consistent with what you saw on the ground?", is because that is the procedure that the Chamber has adopted. I would be happy to put in more of the documents without requiring that they be put in through a witness altogether in most instances. That has been our position for a long time, as the Chamber knows. There are, in having said that, there are instances in which it is helpful indeed to ask the witness to confirm that when a document, a report, an HVO document, an international report, talks about certain things happening in their area, it's helpful, in our submission, to have some of the witnesses confirm that indeed that is exactly -- that is what their experience was. I think that's helpful for the Chamber. I think it's helpful for the proof in the court. So we will continue to look at that. And we always try to narrow, I can assure the Chamber with every witness it is part of our daily exercise to narrow the number of exhibits used with witnesses. We do that every day. In terms of marking -- marking particular passages, Your Honour, we will look further, consider that further. On that and the proofing note, I would just make the following general comment: I asked the Chamber to please understand, and I ask the Defence to understand, because some day a few months from now the shoe will be on the other foot, so to speak. We constantly add to the burdens of the trial teams and the support staff, do this, mark that, summarise this, mark it differently, put it on -- put it in e-court, put it on the ELMO, mark it differently, mark it a second time. It gets very, very time-consuming, Your Honour, to do all these things. None of these things happen automatically or without cost and time and effort. Many of our people are working late into the evenings already to be prepared for the next day. So we will look at that. I think that in the vast majority of instances, most of these documents are 1, 2, 3 pages. The passage is whether -- evident. It takes almost no time at all to deal with it in court, so I would ask the Court to be sensitive to the realities of the burdens placed on the parties in doing this. As to photographs, indeed, Your Honour, if -- if in the last day or two there's been a photo or two shown that probably wasn't necessary I'll certainly speak to the trial team about that. Again, we talk about the narrowing of exhibits every day and if that was done perhaps we could improve on that. However, there are times, as everyone in the courtroom has said, when it is helpful to ask a witness to elaborate on a photograph and what is shown. So there again it's a case-by-case basis. I don't think a lot of time, frankly, is being wasted on it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I note that you're not against these suggestions. You'll try and improve the procedure. I personally would like to add that as far as the evidence is concerned, it's not the quantity used that results in quality evidence. What is important is to have the appropriate evidence. A minute ago with regard to the division of responsibilities between the ABiH and the HVO, the Defence addressed this. There was a document, 1900, that shows that there was an HVO zone of responsibility. It would have been useful for the Judges if the Defence had then shown the witness the document on the agreement between the HVO and the ABiH or the document from the ABiH on the division of responsibilities so that these two documents could be compared, you see. In such cases this procedure is useful, and we could save time. Perhaps you will do this later, I don't know, but perhaps that would have been a good occasion to say to the witness there is a division of responsibilities. I'll show you an ABiH document that shows that outside the -- of the Rotimlje zone of responsibility, there was another area of responsibility. Would you agree with me. That's how we could proceed. Yes, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do agree with you but I can tell you why I hadn't prepared anything of that kind for this witness. It's because I had been told that I was trying to discuss military matters with the witnesses who were victims and who had no military expertise. I believed it wouldn't have been appropriate for me to appear with a map depicting the zone of responsibilities for the Knez Domagoj Brigade and the Bregava Brigade, but otherwise I absolutely agree with you that such a procedure would be very useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I fully concur with Ms. Alaburic, because we realise that these are crime-base witnesses, and that's why we -- we sometimes object to them being asked technical questions or to verify something in a document which they clearly, clearly cannot verify. But if we were, for instance, to adopt something of a procedure I'm suggesting, then obviously the Defence could also have the documents ready and we could have them at the same time We don't have to go through the witness. We could just say, Here are some documents to consider along with this. Otherwise we will do it through our witnesses. But there are ways, I think, to make it easier for you to look at both sides at the same time as the process goes along. I'm not quite so sure with all of Mr. Scott's observations that things are not -- are going rosy and that we're not wasting too much time. I think some time is being wasted. I'm not being critical. But I think I'm having one of those, you know, moments of clarity where I'm seeing perhaps, now that I see the process as it's going, I'm willing to be more flexible and acknowledge that the Prosecution perhaps was right in trying to introduce documents in an easier fashion. Having said that, our concern has always been, what part of the document are they really interested in? Because if they want to bring in a hundred pages or a thousand pages we need to know what paragraphs. And this system now pins them down and it goes directly to your earlier ruling that you will only consider the part of the document that they're looking at -- that they're referring to. So I don't see where the dilemma is, but I'm sure, perhaps with some thought, reasonable minds can come to a reasonable solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: With your permission, Mr. President, I'd like to make a personal statement. I shall not be in the courtroom when the next witness will be heard, although I will still be around, but I have to leave very early tomorrow morning, and it is expected that the witness will still be heard tomorrow morning. I do not think that it would be fair to the Defence if I heard direct examination live but cross-examination only by reading the transcript. I could also be tempted to interfere in the first half and then would be absent in the other. So that's my explanation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You sound like a Defence lawyer, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is 20 to 11.00. We have to have a half-hour break again for the transcript. So we reconvene at 10 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, madam. We're going to move into private session straight away.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, is it correct that prior to the 1st of July, 1993, you and your family and other Muslims in the village of Visici lived in relative peace up until that point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: However, on the 1st of July, 1993, your husband and son were arrested at your home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Correct. At 4.00, in 1993, on the 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Judges what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: At 4.00 on the 1st of July, HVO soldiers turned up at my door. They knocked on the door, asked me to open the door, which I did straight away, asked me if there were any male members. I told them straight away. They went into my house. They wanted to wake my son up. I said I would wake him up. The other soldier went to wake up my husband. I woke my son up quickly and explained to him that he had to get up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you say 4.00. Is that 4.00 a.m.? I assume since they were sleeping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the morning at 4.00, 4.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. So you said you woke up your son. They came to you and asked if there were any men in the house, you woke up your son, and what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: They said they had to go with them. And as their mother, I asked why. And one of the soldiers said that one of his friends had died in Bijelo Polje. I said, "That wasn't my menfolk. They did not do that. They were at home." But my comment led to nothing. The man shouted at my husband, hurried him up. And at that moment I handed some food to my son. The man said that he didn't need any food because breakfast was waiting for them where they were going. And then when we were standing on the threshold, he said, "And whose are these other houses?" I said, "My neighbours." Or, rather, he said, "Is this your neighbour's house?" I kept silent and I said they -- afterwards I said, "They are Croatian houses and they're of no interest to you." They took them away, and I did not know where at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you a couple of questions further about that. Can you tell the Judges, please, around the 1st of July, 1993, perhaps both in the previous day or two and on the 1st of July itself, was there any fighting or combat operations in the village or the immediate area of the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, not in the village and not in the immediate area around the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Had either your son or your husband engaged in any type of military activities around this time, the 1st of July, 1993; if ever, but at this particular time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Not before, not then, not after, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The soldiers who came to your home at 4.00 in the morning on the 1st of July, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: They were dressed in camouflage uniforms, and they had various colours painted on their face, thick paints.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you see any badges or insignia or other markings on any parts of their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The HVO insignia.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just looking ahead for a moment, madam. Can you tell us that -- your husband and son were taken away on the 1st of July, 1993. When did you first receive any information as to what had become of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: I learnt half an hour later where they had been taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And where was that, please, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: My son's school friend passed by my house and I asked him, and he told me that everybody had been taken to Dretelj, to some sort of storage, fuel storage, facility that used to belong to the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And again, please, looking ahead, and we'll come back to this toward the end of your testimony, but when did you next see your husband again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: On the 2nd of April, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And when did you next see your son, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: The 1st of August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What did you do after your son and husband were taken away? On that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Just like any other woman, I tried to organised my life as best I could. I went around doing housework.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did it come to are attention on that day or around that time that not only your husband and son had been arrested and taken away but the other Muslim men in your village had been in a similar way arrested and taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I did see that with my very own eyes when they took an old man away and a friend of his who lived with him. He was some sort of refugee from Srebrenica. I saw that with my own eyes, because my house is not far from that neighbour's house.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But did a group of soldiers either come to your house or one of your neighbour's houses around this time, that is sometime on the 1st of July, after your husband and son were arrested?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My apology. Did you observe any soldiers coming to one of your neighbour's houses? And again, I caution you not to mention names, but did you see a group of soldiers come to any of your neighbour's houses around this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've already said that I saw them come to the house of that neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us anybody more what happened? Were any of the people at that house taken away, beaten? What did you see happen there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I saw a group of soldiers take these two old men away. They were in front and behind. One of the old men was saying something, and a soldier rushed up to him, hit him with his rifle butt and said that he should keep quiet, that he would otherwise kill him and throw him on the rubbish heap.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, specifically, later that same day, did soldiers come to your house and conduct a search there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, madam, I'm going to ask you to tell us what happened there, and at a certain point I'm going to ask to stop and go into private session, but can you tell us first of all just generally what happened when the soldiers came there, and then I'll be listening for your answer and at some point we'll need to go into private session, but can you tell us what happened, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. A red car turned up, a van, stopped in front of my house, and out of the van came three soldiers. They entered my yard. I was there with my two daughters. They asked me to hand over a pistol, a pistol I did not have. The soldier said to me that my husband had owned up and said that we had a pistol. Of course I said he couldn't have owned up to anything like that. He called me to come inside the house, into the bedroom, to be more precise --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to stop you there, madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, yes, before we go into private session, on the basis of what you've said, and I've understood at 4.00 in the morning two soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms, with paint on their face, different coloured paint on their face, like Rambo, entered your house and took your husband away. That might have taken half an hour. It was -- so that was by that time half past 4.00 or 5.00 in the morning. Then you said that you saw other people. So what time was this, 5.00 in the morning, 6.00, 7.00, 8.00 in the morning, in the afternoon? Could you be more precise on that point, the time. And tell us when this car arrived with the three individuals. What time was that? Can you enlighten us to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honours. It was at about 10.00 of that same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So when the vehicle arrived it was 10.00 in the morning. And when you saw your neighbours being taken off, that was before 10.00, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was at around 5.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's move into private session for a few moments.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, madam, I'm going -- just to be very clear, we're back in open session now, so whatever you're going to say now will be broadcast, so please be mindful of that in terms of any names or other matters that you might consider sensitive. So you said at this point there was continued activity around the house. You went outside. "A second soldier came out of our garage," you said. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: He said that there was nothing to be found there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was there anything said about setting the garage on fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes. At that point in time, I said they could set it on fire but that there were Croatian houses surrounding the house. The other soldier told them to hit me and not to allow me to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what happened after that? Anything more you can say that you don't feel needs to be in private session? What happened at that time? Did anything happen to your car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Ah, yes. A soldier took his rifle. He broke up the tank. He took a canister from their car, took some fuel. They also took some other items from the car, but I don't know what.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, at this time I'll ask to move back into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, again we're back in open session, so I caution you again not to say anything you said in private session. However, just to follow up on what the Judge said. I'm not asking about what happened. But can you tell the Judges, did you have phone service at your house as of the 1st of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, naturally I had a phone, but the phone stopped working on the 1st of July. At 4.15 I tried to make a phone call and the phone wasn't working.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you find later on that day or on a subsequent day that in the houses where your Croat neighbours lived, that your Croat names did have phone service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: After that point in time did you begin to stay with various of your neighbours and friends after the 1st of July, 1993, in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't sleep in my house after that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And this also included your children, I take it, who were with you. Again, don't mention their names, but they were also travelling with you from place to place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes, of course. What kind of mother would I have been if I had left my children behind?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you find -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, I want to go back to the issue of the telephone, which I'm particularly interested in. The soldiers arrived at 4.00 in the morning. It was dark. Everyone was an asleep. And at 4.15 you said you tried to make a phone cull. I assume you tried to make a phone call after they had left and you said that the phone wasn't working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So tell me when did you phone or when did you try to make a phone call, at what time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My husband and son were taken away very rapidly. It was perhaps 4.20 when I tried to phone Capljina in a state of shock. I wanted to phone some friends or my sister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When did you ask your Croatian neighbours whether their telephone lines were functioning properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps two days later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And their phones were functioning two days later. Yours never worked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Although you are not a technician, did you ever ask yourself why your phone was not working, since the phones in the neighbouring houses were? Did you check to see if the telephone lines had been cut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in an hour's time the Bosniak women found out that no one's phones were working. It wasn't just a matter of my telephone line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So all the Muslim houses no longer had telephones functioning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in the Croatian houses the phones were working.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And no one tried to find out how this happened, whether it was a matter of the telephone exchange or whether the telephone exchange itself had been concerned or that the houses --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're not such a stupid people. We immediately knew that an order had been issued to cut the telephone lines that belonged to the Bosniaks. It really wasn't necessary to look into anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you knew that an order had been issued. Who told you that an order had been issued?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in spite of all of the orders, I lived in an honourable manner and in an honest manner. For 18 years I had very good friends of Croat ethnicity, and it wasn't possible to order everything. It wasn't possible to order me to say certain things.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, in connection with what you've told us so far, but can you just confirm again, when you began to move around later on the 1st of July and in the days thereafter, did you find this there were other Muslim or Bosniak families in the village, women and children, who, again, the men from their families had been taken away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I found out about all of this by perhaps 8.00 in the part of Visici that I lived in. That's when I found out that they had all been taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in -- on that -- on that day and the days thereafter, can you tell us that -- was any of the property of your family or your neighbour's family, taken by anyone? Stolen, looted, however you'd like to describe it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Nothing was taken from my family.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And how about your neighbours and perhaps relatives? And again without mentioning names, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: I saw them taking away some vehicles that belonged to refugees from Stolac.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you see any property or boxes, what have you, being removed or carried out of houses in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: I saw that from a house that no one was living in at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you saw happen in connection with the items being removed from that particular house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: They were putting things in the car. The number plates were the number plates of vehicles from Makarska. They weren't the owners of the house since I knew the owner. I don't know what they took away, but I did see these parcels.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And were the men -- were the persons, excuse me, that got out of these vehicles and were removing these parcels, did they have uniforms on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
