utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And were you -- can you tell us, were you sufficiently close to these events that you could hear any of these individuals speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges whether you recognised any particular accent of the people -- soldiers that you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: They were speaking in the Dalmatian dialect. We lived very close to Metkovici, and I was well aware of the way in which Dalmatians spoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm to the Judges, please, it may be as simple as looking at a happen, but is Metkovici in the Republic of Croatia? Is Metkovici in the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And can you just -- just to conclude on this, can you tell the Judges approximately how many times you say that -- you saw this same group of soldiers come and remove items from this house that you've described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: I saw those soldiers come two to three times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you've said a moment ago that the soldiers spoke a dialect, that they had a Dalmatian accent, and then you said that you knew that. Could you tell me what the Dalmatian dialect is like? Or, rather, do you know the accent, and for what reason? Could you tell us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we say, "gdje si," where are you? And the Dalmatians say, "di si." There are many examples, words I can differentiate. So it's easily recognisable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So having heard them speak in that way, what was your conclusion as to where they came from? Where could they have come from, to your mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could have been from Metkovici or from Croatia or -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And my last question, because this is important for us Judges. When you saw them, these men taking the stuff from your house, putting them into their truck and so on, what time was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it wasn't always the same time. Once they came in the morning. Another time they were it there at noon. The third time -- well, I can't really remember the exact time because, Your Honour, I didn't have much time to look at the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So on the first occasion it was the morning, and on one occasion it was in the afternoon. Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm moving to another topic, and if we could go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, proceed. Yes, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, before continuing on with certain other events in July, can you tell the Judges, after the 1st of July, approximately how many Muslim women and children remained in the village after the men are taken away, or most of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can speak about the part of the village where I lived. There might have been during that period of time women, children, and elderly, about 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: During this time did you witness anything happen to -- and I'm not mentioning names, but to the father of one of your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, again without using his name, was this man approximately 70 years old at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges what you saw happen to this individual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: There was a curfew on, so that from 10.00 in the evening until 6.00 in the morning we weren't allowed to move around anywhere. We weren't allowed to leave our houses. This old man came to sleep in his daughter's house, and she was my neighbour, and I slept there too. So he went to his own house to have a shower, to bathe. At a certain point in time we heard shooting, and we heard terrible screams and someone shouting, "Help, help." We did not know what was going on. And since it's a village with one-storey houses, we looked out the window and saw a half-naked man running down the street. He crossed the street -- or, rather, passed by the front door of my neighbour's house and stopped. Slowly we watched that man and saw that he was in fact my neighbour's father. She started shouting out, "Father, father," and I had to go out with her. The man was half naked. He was bleeding from his head. He had been beaten. We brought him into the house. He groaned and moaned and cried. We asked him what had happened, and he said he had gone into the bathroom to have a shower. He said someone started bashing on the bathroom door. He opened the door and saw soldiers standing outside. They told him that he had to give them money. He went out of the bathroom and started unlocking the door to the room and it was at that point that he managed to escape from that soldier. However, in running across his yard to the street, he came upon another soldier who hit him with his rifle butt in his -- on his head, on his ear, and his ear started bleeding, and he started groaning and moaning, and then the man beat him all over his body. And we spent the whole night putting ointment and -- on his body and balms. And in the morning his daughter found somebody to take him to a doctor. He was examined by the doctor, and he had three broken ribs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, madam, before we move on, you've mentioned a curfew. Can you tell the Judges when this curfew was imposed and who imposed, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not know when the curfew was introduced exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: However, we learnt from our neighbours that the curfew was in force. Now, who issued the order, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you hear the curfew announced or discussed on radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course. And we were told not to open the door to anybody coming by at night after 10.00 p.m., anybody who came to your yard or in front of your door.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And do you know which radio station broadcast this report or announcement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Croatian radio. The station in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And can you tell the Judges who -- based on what you saw and observed, who enforced the curfew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I really can't say who enforced the curfew. All I can tell you is that we adhered to the curfew.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it then. It may be a question -- my poor question or it may be a question of translation. Did you see people who would go around at night to make sure that the curfew was being kept or complied with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes. Soldiers did pass by fairly often.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about another incident. Again, please don't mention any names, but did there come a time when one of your other neighbours had indicated that money had been taken from her? If you recall that, then I'm just going to ask you to briefly describe what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes. One night, I don't remember the date, at 2.30 a.m., they came knocking at my neighbour's door, and I was sleeping in their house. They said, "Open up. Police." Of course we complied straight away. They entered the house, and we had some bags that had been prepare. The bags were searched straight away. I had an eight-month old -- I was holding an eight-month old baby belonging to my neighbour. And they said they were searching the houses, looking for weapons. I told the soldiers that my house was locked, and could I go and open the door for them, with them, and he said yes. And my neighbour's house and her father's house was locked, too, and they allowed my neighbour to go. We stopped by a house. It was a Muslim house belonging to the Basaric family, and they were supposed to search that house too. Well, they did, and we stayed outside on the street. We heard a lot of noise, things falling, being thrown about. They said that they'd found a man, a male. And later on, it turned out that they didn't take him away because he was a 16 -- it was a 16-year-old boy, a minor. And his mother showed them his medical record card proving that. So while I was standing outside with one of the soldiers and my neighbour, a female neighbour -- a male neighbour of mine came by who was a school friend of my son's. He wasn't wearing a uniform on the occasion, and I asked him to help me go and unlock my own house straight away so that my children should not be -- should not be afraid for my life, and he agreed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My apology. Let me interrupt you for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do see in the transcript that one name was mentioned. I don't think it's necessary -- I don't think the situation is such that it's necessary to redact it. I do, however, just want to stop to caution the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Please be careful about the use of names, madam. So you've just told us that you wanted your house to be unlocked so that your children would not be afraid again. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: The young man went with me and with another soldier. We arrived at my house, unlocked the door. The soldier started searching the house, this young man. My neighbour asked me then -- asked me again whether I had any weapons, and I answered him as I would my own child. I said that I had no weapons, and if I had a golden cannon I would have given it to them, because I have nothing to hide in my house because my son and my husband weren't there, and I don't know what I'd do with a weapon. And he told the other soldier who was busy searching the house that everything was all right, that he needn't search the house any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me direct your attention to -- during this time when these soldiers were coming and -- did you come again -- excuse me, across an individual that you -- or you recognised a particular accent or dialect being used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes. I did not recognise him. He was older are than the young men but also spoke in the Dalmatian dialect. They listened to him; he issued orders. Who the man was, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You've said just now that the others listened to him. Let me just follow up. Did the other men who were around this man who spoke with a Dalmatian accent or dialect, did they treat him differently than they did each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what did you see again in that respect? In what way did they treat him differently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: He said, "Don't hurry. You'll lose your head that way if you hurry too much." Then they went back. They'd obey. They would say, "Yes. Very well."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention now, please, to the mosque in your village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, just very briefly could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, madam, is it correct that there was a mosque in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And we're going to go through these next events in some detail, but in the course of the time we're talking about now, was the mosque destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We've been talking since this morning about July, 1993. Was the mosque in the village destroyed during this time? I don't think your answer was picked up on the record, madam.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Up until July, well, no, the mosque hadn't been destroyed by then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I apologise. There might be an error in either my question or the translation. Was the mosque in your village destroyed sometime in July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And can you just tell us about that, please, again not mentioning any particular names, but the sequence of events surrounding that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps the date won't be correct. At the time, I only counted the amount of time my family members had spent in the camp. That's how I found my bearings. But I know around 4.00 in the afternoon on one day, a red Golf vehicle stopped on the M17 road, which is perhaps 20 metres from the mosque. I saw that because I was standing in front of my neighbour's house. Four soldiers got out of the car. They were in military uniforms. They rapidly crossed the road and reached the mosque. They broke the windows and threw something into the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In -- sorry, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: And similarly, they quickly returned to the car and drove off in the direction of Metkovici. They took the main road. And a short while later you could hear an explosion. There were two explosions for sure, but I'm not sure whether there were more than two. There were fewer than five explosions though.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In terms of the date, madam, if I can direct your attention, as a benchmark, the 1st of July which we've talked about extensively today, approximately how far after that do you remember this first incident concerning the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Well, 13 or 14 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. So approximately in mid-July, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And when you said that you heard these explosions after the vehicle drove away, what else could you observe about the mosque around that time? What was the state of damage, if any? What more can you tell the Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: The windows had been broken. You could hear the sound of glass shattering, and a little later I passed through a yard and through the window. I saw a carpet by the wall. I couldn't see the floor. You could feel the smell of wool burning. I assumed that the carpets were burning, but there wasn't really a fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, was there any -- were there any further incidents concerning the mosque after that occasion, the occasion that you've just described to us now? Did anything else happen to the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Not long after -- well, I was also sleeping at my neighbour's. Her house was near the mosque. And between 3.00 and 4.00 in the morning I was woken up by the sound of a loud explosion. I could hear a metallic sound. I immediately ran out to the balcony of her house, and from that point I could see the mosque quite clearly. I saw that the walls of the mosque were like cardboard, and there was no roof. The mosque had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was the state of the minaret as of that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: The minaret remained standing. It wasn't linked to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Judges, around this time did you find any -- did you receive any information in the village from your neighbours, from -- I'll ask you in a moment to say who, but did you receive any information that the minaret was then going to be destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Without mentioning a name now, can you just tell us what you learned in that regard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes. When the mosque was destroyed on that day, the weather on the following day was terrible. It was raining, and nothing in particular happened. The day after, so two days after, I met a neighbour, and the neighbour told me that I shouldn't sleep in the vicinity of the mosque together with my children, because that night the minaret would be blown up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Again without mentioning a name, madam, can you tell the Judges was this neighbour a Bosniak or a Croat neighbour?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: The neighbour was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And later on that night, did you observe anything in the village that you would tell the Judges about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: As I knew what was going to happen that night, I also informed my Bosniak neighbours of the fact that we had to go and sleep elsewhere, and I told them the reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you see any vehicles moving around the village that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I saw a vehicle driving around, and it stopped by every Croatian house in the vicinity of the mosque, where it passed by every Croatian house in the vicinity of the mosque and went even further.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you -- again, before we get to what happened to the mosque but in connection with this vehicle that was moving from Croat house to Croat house, did you hear any time the next day or the day after about what had been happening in this connection as far as you were told?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, naturally my neighbour told me that on that night the inhabitants of Croatian houses were told that they should open their windows to avoid damage of any kind. Naturally, the Bosniaks were not informed of anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And then going back to the night itself, what happened in connection with the minaret?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: At about midnight it was absolutely quiet. There was no traffic. You couldn't hear anything. We knew something was going to happen, and I have already told you why. And at about 1.00 the ground shook a bit. It was a little like a mild earthquake. Then you could hear the sound of a loud explosion. Naturally, we knew what was happening. And perhaps a few minutes later cars started driving down the road. There were shouts of joy. You could hear shots. People were celebrating.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell, madam -- could you tell the Judges, could you tell which of the ethnic groups in the village were celebrating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll tell you, although I don't believe it's essential. The Croats were celebrating.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'd like to object to the question about which ethnic group was celebrating an event. Only people can celebrate an event, not an ethnic group.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what did you see the next morning, madam, in connection with what had happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, I saw the destroyed minaret. It had been toppled over. And in the vicinity of the mosque there were some Croatian houses. There was damage that had been inflicted on the houses. A car arrived. Men in civilian uniforms got out of the car. The car was from the municipality of Capljina. The people were from the municipality. I don't know their names, but before the war I went to the municipality. I had certain things to sort out in the municipality, just like everyone else. They had come to record the damage.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you saw these individuals who came to record the damage, which structures or houses did they look at?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I have already said, they focused their attention on the Croatian houses. They were in the vicinity. There were also two Bosniak house. There were more Croatian houses, however, and these are the houses that they focused their attention on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you see during that time whether they focused any attention on either the Muslim houses or the mosque?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: They didn't, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So the record is entirely clear on this point hopefully, madam, can you tell the Judges around the time that the mosque was destroyed during mid-July, 1993, were there any military operation, any fighting in your village going on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the time there was no fighting in our village or in the surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, around this time, madam, did you see a particular individual that you recognised as a senior Croat or Bosnian Croat officer, official, come into the village or pass by your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: I'm not sure how much time had passed. Perhaps several days, but certainly not more than a month, because I only spent a month in Visici after my husband and son had been arrested. I went in the direction of the M17 road from our street, and I saw a car there. The car was moving but very slowly, and I saw General Praljak in the car. He was sitting by the other person in the front. He was five metres away from me, so I could see him quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Praljak in the driver's seat or was he in the passenger's seat of the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: He was next to the passenger.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, next to the passenger? Was he driving the vehicle? Was Mr. Praljak driving the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So is it correct, ma'am, that there was a driver in the vehicle and seated next to the driver in the front passenger's seat was the person you identified as Mr. Slobodan Praljak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges how it was that you were able to identify Mr. Praljak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the time General Praljak made frequent appearances on television. We often watched Croatian television, and as a result I was able to recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you observe Mr. Praljak making any motions or indications with his hand inside the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object to the leading nature of that question. I mean, now we're getting to a rather, I would say, important aspect of her testimony, and so he can ask the question, what did she see, and she can describe.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm happy to do so, Your Honour. I'll rephrase the question. I think -- I'm not going to belabour it, Your Honour. I'm happy --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What did you see at the time you saw Mr. Praljak at this location a short distance away from you? Tell the Judges what you saw.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: As the car was moving very slowly, I saw General Praljak, and as they were driving down the main road the general made this sort of a gesture with his hand, and he was pointing at the mosque. Is that fine? Is that all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Is your headset --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: He pointed at the mosque. Everything is fine. The lead's a little short, but it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the interruption there. What -- can you just say again what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: I saw a car moving slowly. General Praljak was sitting in the passenger's seat. As they passed by the mosque, the General made a sign with his hand, this sort of a sign.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please, now that we know what we're -- the Judges are looking for and we're all looking for, can you show us again the motion that you saw Mr. Praljak make? And when Mr. Praljak made this motions -- and let the record reflect the witness has made a downward motion with her arm from -- going from an upward position to a lowered position?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That wasn't quite the way I saw it, Your Honour. I wonder whether we could have the motion again, then, to be clear about that and perhaps have a specific description for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would be happy to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will describe the gesture. She made a circular gesture with her right hand. Could you do that again? Could you make the gesture again so that everyone can see it? Her right hand was initially at the level of her left arm, and she drew a circle.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the time when this motion was made, was this motion also made in any particular direction and, if so, in what direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: The -- he used his right and to make this motion, and the -- towards the right, and the mosque was to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does that mean, madam, that the mosque was in the direction his right hand was pointing at after he had made this circular motion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may intervene for a second. This is exactly what I'm talking about, a waste of time, because she doesn't know when. We don't have an exact period, and we have a gesture, a car that's going slowly, we don't know how long. We don't know what the conversation was. What weight, if any, can this be given from this witness? In my opinion, none. And we're wasting valuable time and spending on this -- this sort of flimsy evidence that somehow the Prosecution wishes to tie Mr. Praljak with -- with the destruction of the mosque. I find this somewhat absurd.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I couldn't disagree more. Mr. Karnavas can argue his case later. Of course he can, and he can also cross-examine the witness. But the witness has given her evidence and I think everyone in the courtroom's been able to see it and hear it, and any comments that Mr. Karnavas has now made goes clearly purely to weight. And of course the witnesses will consider the evidence along with all other evidence in the case to decide how determine how the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on to other subjects.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, can you tell the Judges before we leave this topic, when you saw Mr. Praljak make this motion toward the mosque at this time, what was the -- where in the sequence of events and the destruction of the mosque was it before the mosque was destroyed, during the episodes you've told us about today, or after the mosque was destroyed? As best you can assist us, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: I think that the mosque had already been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When did you then come to leave -- or did you leave your village sometime toward the end of July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Where did you go at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: I went to my sister's in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a question. You spoke of General Praljak, and you said yourself "General Praljak." That's how you referred to him. How did you know him? How did you know that it was General Praljak? How did you know exactly that he was a general and that this was General Praljak? Because we -- you can see lots of people pass by in a car without saying, "Hold on a minute, that's X, Y, or Z."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the car was moving very slowly, and I've already said that every night or almost every night we saw on television -- we watched General Praljak on television. And I remember faces like him and personalities like him very well. At that time, General Praljak was not unknown, and I knew it was the general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because you saw him on television.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was your -- were your televisions working at that time in July in your village? Did you have television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we did have television. It was working. We did have electricity, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you had electricity. And it was television broadcast from where, Zagreb, Mostar, Sarajevo? Where was the broadcasting coming from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was Zagreb television, Your Honour, from Zagreb. THE PROSECUTOR:

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, moving forward then. Before you left your village, I was taking you to the time when you left the village, but before that, can you tell the Judges whether you learned anything about this time about the possibility of Muslim men being released from detention. There was some way that might be accomplished and, if so, please describe that to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: We heard that liberation was possible if you had a letter of guarantee to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What did you understand this letter of guarantee to involve or relate to? A letter of guarantee to do what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: That my husband and son would be released and that they -- well, maybe I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, if they would be released, then what would happen to them according to this letter of guarantee? Where would they go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, they would go to the country from where I got the letter of guarantee from.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How did you learn about this arrangement, that the Muslim men could be released if they went to a third country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: I can't remember who told me this personally, but I realised -- I saw, actually that women were already going, looking for their relatives, calling up their relatives and friends abroad to help them, to send letters of guarantee and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, going back to the time when you left your village, again please don't mention any names, but you then moved to the town of Capljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And approximately when was that in terms of -- again, how long after your husband and son were arrested on 1st of July? How long after that did you move to Capljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Well, one or two months.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Capljina approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Until the 23rd of August, 1993, when I had to leave Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come to that in a moment. When you went to Capljina, I take it it's perhaps obvious, but again we can't assume too much for the purposes of the record. When you went to Capljina, you took your children with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges when you went to -- excuse me. When you went to Capljina did anyone say anything to you during that time about your children going to school in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: While I was at my sister's place, one night two ladies came by. They were Croatian. They knocked on the door and went into her home. One of those women, I didn't ask her name and I don't know what her name is, but she told my sister that she had brought a friend of hers along from Siroki Brijeg and that they wanted to take up residence in her home because our children would not be going, that is to say the Bosniak children would not be going to school as of the 1st of September. So she said that as we were leaving anyway, then her friend could move into her sister's place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What's gone in the transcript, madam, is Realtime? "take up residence in her home because our children would not shall going," I'm sorry, but would you clarify again what was said about your children going to school in Capljina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Your Honours, the children would go back to school on the 1st of September every year, and this lady who came by said that -- and since that was the month of August that our children come September wouldn't be going to school. Our children, the Bosniak children, wouldn't be going to school in Capljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I might, I'm coming to the last topic of the examination and that is the -- what happens in Capljina and then the expulsions from Capljina. I will not be able to finish that in five minutes. I note that so far I've used approximately 1 hour and 29 minutes, but I would request from the Chamber if we can stop now and I'll finish this final part in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't use the five minutes? Let me give you a demonstration. She can say a whole lot of things in five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll be happy to, Your Honour. If the Court wishes to proceed that way, I'll be happy to.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, if you could turn your attention then you told us a few moments ago that around the 23rd of August, 1993, you were removed -- I don't know your exact word now, and it's no longer in the transcript that I can see, but that you were moved out of Capljina. Can you tell the Judges what happened at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Yes. On the 23rd of August, in the afternoon, it might have been 5.00 or 6.00 p.m., in front of my sister's place a police vehicle turned up with megaphones, and it called upon the Muslim citizens to step outside their front doors.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The police vehicle that was broadcasting this direction was -- could you tell could you see any markings on the police vehicle or could you tell the Judges what police were active in Capljina in August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: At that time it was a police car belonging to the civilian police, the police we had -- the police force we had up until then. It was a police vehicle, a police car. How else can I describe it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. And what did you do, you and others do after hearing this announcement over the megaphone to -- for all Muslims to go out in front of the houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: We were so frightened that we complied with the order straight away. I and my children set out straight away, stepped outside. And in front of the door there was a car waiting, a heavy-duty vehicle. My sister took a while, and two policemen entered through the entrance. I asked her why she had taken so long, and she said that she had to hand over the keys to her home. We got into the car straight away, into the vehicle straight away, and there were lots of residents in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Before you go further, madam, when you say that your sister said that she had to turn over the keys to her home, had to turn her keys over to who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: To those policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you said you got in a vehicle straight away, and there were lots of residents in the vehicle. What type of vehicle did you get into at that time? You said it was a heavy duty vehicle. Was it a truck of some sort?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: It was a two-tonne truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And by the time the truck was full, if you will, approximately how many people would you say were in the back of this truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Perhaps 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And where were you taken in the truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: They took us to the Lasta Silos, the Lasta company from Capljina, the Silos.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what happened when you arrived at the Silos?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: There were already lots of women and children and elderly people there. The Silo was composed of several parts, chambers, rooms. I don't know. Any way, they were all full. And at the end of the corridor there was just enough room for us too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say, madam that, there were already lots of women and elderly people there, can you give us an approximate number as best you can, 50, 100, any estimate how many people you saw there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: Well, there might have been perhaps 150 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what happened to you after you were take -- you and the others in your truck -- in the truck you were on -- excuse me, what happened after you arrived at the Silos? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CO
utterances.text: We took the personal belongings we had with us and went to the Silo, and at about 10.00 the transport from the Silo started. Trucks turned up and the people would get into them again. My children, my daughter, she was eight years old at the time. She was absolutely petrified. She would go around hugging all the women in the Silo, asking them whether they would kill us. Nobody showed too much emotion at that time. They didn't take the trouble to console my child. And people didn't know behalf going to happen. So I took my two daughters around me, and I heard the order shouted out, "Throw away everything you've brought with you." There was a lot of swearing and shooting going on in the corridor. And a soldier asked for a knife. I didn't know what he needed a knife for. Later on, I learnt that an old man had brought a canister of water with him, and the soldier asked for a knife to pour the water out. And that was the night that I boarded the truck and left the Silo with my children. It was about 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, yes. Do you need more time tomorrow, Mr. Scott, or have you finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I will need maybe probably approximately -- I would say approximately 10 minutes on just general questions, and then there are about five or six documents to show to the witness, including a video. The video will show what happened concerning these vehicles. So I do think it will take some time. I note at the moment I'm at one hour, 35 minutes, so I'm well under the two hours that we estimated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We adjourn until tomorrow morning at 9.00. Now, with respect to the legionnaires disease bacteria, we still have not received any update on the report from the experts, so we'll let you know in due course as soon as we learn anything more. The situation is under control, however, and there is no danger. We reconvene tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of December, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
